Triggers.value: When people say things like my ex

Maladaptive Strategies.value: make sure to stay close to exit
Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

issues.explanation: 'Heavy make-up' is hard to reconcile with this patient's demographics (22-year-old single male auditor) and the rest of the profile unless there is a specific unreported context such as concealment or gender expression. In this profile it stands out as clinically implausible relative to the other items, whereas the other maladaptive strategies center on vigilance, escape, and social evaluation.

vignette: Ahmed, a 22‑year‑old auditor of Lebanese descent, worked in a bustling downtown office. When he was nineteen, a senior colleague who had been invited to a client dinner took advantage of the crowded, dimly lit room to force himself upon Ahmed. The moment is still fresh in his mind: the metallic tang of the air conditioning, the lingering perfume of the room’s freshly scented candles, and the sudden, sharp movement of the man’s arm as he pushed past Ahmed’s shoulder. The violation was not only physical but moral; Ahmed had been the one who had opened the door for the man and had trusted him as a colleague and a friend. Those sensations—especially the smell of the candles, the man's abrupt movement, and the sense that someone was misbehaving—have become the very triggers that keep him trapped in the aftermath. After the assault, Ahmed began to notice that certain odors—any scent he associated with a locker room or a conference room—would snap him into a state of hypervigilance. The smell itself, or the mere thought of a similar odor, would lead him to rush to the nearest exit, to avoid situations where others might evaluate his performance or appearance, and to dress in concealing clothing that could hide any signs of bruising or stress. He also avoided unfamiliar places, preferring the familiarity of his own office and the routine of audit rooms he had spent years inspecting. The threat of sudden movements and the possibility that any stranger might turn a benign interaction into an assault kept his body constantly tense, a physical reminder that danger lurked behind every door. These reactions are exactly the maladaptive strategies that stem directly from the triggers: when the smell of a candle rises, Ahmed’s first instinct is to stay near an exit, to wear layered clothing, and to keep his eyes peeled for any odd movement. The very act of avoiding the triggers also fed into his negative self‑appraisals. Ahmed began to compare himself to others, thinking that someone more careful or more powerful would not have allowed such an event to happen. He could not shake the feeling that he had somehow failed to keep himself safe. The realization that the people he had trusted—his former friends, the clients he had served—could no longer be trusted eroded his sense of joy. The humiliation of being violated in a place where he had been praised for his diligence left him feeling permanently degraded. The weight of those thoughts—lost happiness, humiliation, and self‑comparison—reinforced his belief that he was the only one who could not protect himself. Maladaptive strategies also amplified Ahmed’s negative appraisals. By constantly staying near exits and concealing himself, he inadvertently made himself the very person that others would look at and judge; the act of hiding his clothes in a line of bright, casual attire caused him to feel more scrutinized and, in turn, more humiliated. The strategies he employed, meant to protect him, only magnified the feeling that he was different and less capable than his peers. Moreover, the very act of keeping his body in a constant state of readiness heightened his sensitivity to normal office noises and movements, turning ordinary greetings into potential threats. In this way, the strategies he used to cope also became new triggers, turning everyday office chatter into a reminder of the assault and reinforcing his sense of danger. The constant alertness and avoidance, in turn, perpetuated the feeling of threat, creating a cycle that tightened around him day after day. In the weeks that followed, the cycle became more pronounced. At the audit firm, Ahmed avoided taking on new client sites, refusing to go to unfamiliar conference rooms or client meetings. When a junior colleague asked him to review a financial report, he would insist on doing it in the back office, close to the elevator, rather than in the bright conference space. His avoidance of unfamiliar places at work, triggered by the fear that someone could harm him, meant he was no longer meeting deadlines and lost opportunities for promotion. The very environment that once gave him pride now reinforced his sense of inadequacy. His body’s constant tension, triggered by the slightest movement or scent, made every audit session feel like a battle rather than a professional task. Each time he stayed near an exit or covered his clothing, he felt the weight of humiliation grow heavier, his belief that he was “broken” hardening. Now, five years after the assault, Ahmed sits on the threshold of a new job interview, heart hammering, body tense. He has avoided the front desk and the receptionist’s smile, fearful that any evaluation might trigger a memory of the violation. It is this fear of being scrutinized—an echo of the humiliation he feels—that has driven him to seek therapy. He tells his therapist that the most terrifying thought is that he will once again feel like a victim, that the world will view him as weak. Yet he also hopes that by confronting these triggers and the maladaptive strategies that bind him, he can reclaim the sense of joy he lost and rebuild his professional identity.
